claims.text: High-entropy alloys resist simultaneous wear and corrosion because they can form a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer.
A stable passive oxide layer minimizes mechanical degradation.
A stable passive oxide layer minimizes electrochemical attack.
The alloys considered initially have a homogeneous microstructure and no pre-existing surface damage.
The alloy's compositional complexity promotes formation of a protective passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer dynamically repairs disruptions caused by cyclic sliding wear.
The passive oxide barrier limits electrochemical reactions responsible for corrosion.
The passive oxide barrier limits mechanical surface damage from wear.
An alloy capable of stable, self-healing passivation will have lower overall mass loss than a matched alloy lacking robust passivation.
An alloy capable of stable, self-healing passivation will develop shallower wear tracks than the matched baseline.
An alloy capable of stable, self-healing passivation will exhibit reduced corrosion indicators relative to the matched baseline.
The combined degradation rate will be less than the sum of the separately measured wear and corrosion rates.
The predicted benefit should hold at room temperature, moderate chloride concentration, and moderate mechanical load.
Very high or low pH, elevated temperature, or excessive mechanical stress can destabilize the oxide layer.
Destabilization of the oxide layer under extreme conditions will diminish its protective effect.
The magnitude of protection may vary with small changes in alloy composition or test conditions.
